# Operator Mixed Ensembles {#sec-operator-mixed}

::: problem
[]{#prob:Gibbtest label="prob:Gibbtest"} Given access to either (i). A
set of state
${S}_{\mathcal{O}}:=\{(\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon O_x)/d\}_{x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}}$
or (ii) $\rho = \mathbb{I}/2^n$, try to distinguish between these two
cases with an error of at most $1/2-\varepsilon$.
:::

This problem determines the lower bound of classical shadow of
$\{O_x\}_{x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}}$ and has a special case for
discrimination of $\mathbb{I}/d$ and Pauli mixed state
$\rho = (\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon P)/2^n$ with $P \in \mathcal{P}_n$.

We first get intuition of this task based on
Lemma. If we choose distribution on
$\mathcal{O}$ supports on $Z_1$ operators only, we conclude that the
value $\|\mu_1^{(1)} - \mu_2^{(1)}\|_1$ are separately
$\|3\varepsilon Z_1/2^n\|_1 = \mathrm{tr}\left({3\varepsilon \mathbb{I}/2^n}\right) = 3\varepsilon$
and
$$
\|4^{-n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}}3\varepsilon P/2^n\|_1 \\
= 3\varepsilon \left[\mathrm{tr}\left(\sqrt{AA^\dagger}\right) \right]^{n} \\
= 3\varepsilon(\sqrt{3}/2)^n \sim \mathcal{O}(2^{-n}).
$$
Here we use
$\mathrm{tr}\left(\sqrt{AA^\dagger}\right) = \sum_{\lambda(A)}|\lambda(A)|$
and $$\begin{align}
A = \frac{I+X+Y+Z}{4} =4^{-1} \begin{pmatrix}2&1- i\\1+i&0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \lambda(A) = {\frac{1 - \sqrt{3}}{4},\frac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{4}}.
\end{align}$$ This means that even though there exists easy distribution
$\mathrm{Pr}(P)=\delta(P - Z_1)$ on Pauli operators that can be
distinguished with $\mathbb{I}/d$ with single replica strategy, there
also has distribution $\mathrm{Pr}(P) = 4^{-n}$ that might be hard.
Based on this intuition, we set up hard distributions as uniform
distribution on signed operators $\{+1,-1\}\times \mathcal{O}$. This
ensures its average is exactly $\mathbb{I}/d$, thus being hard for
1-replica strategy.

## General Operators {#sec-general-ops}

### Single-Copy Strategy {#sec-single-copy}

For shadow tomography of general operator set $\{O_1,\cdots,O_M\}$ where
$O_j$ is an arbitrary $n$-qubits operator, we build hard distribution by
rotating Pauli $Z$ operators with independent Haar random unitary:
$$\begin{align}
    O_{1},\cdots,O_{M/2} &= U_1Z_1U_1^{\dagger}, \cdots, U_{M/2}Z_{M/2}U_{M/2}^{\dagger},\\
    O_{M/2+1},\cdots,O_{M} &= -U_1Z_1U_1^{\dagger}, \cdots, -U_{M/2}Z_{M/2}U_{M/2}^{\dagger},
\end{align}$$ where $U_1,\cdots,U_{M/2}$ are independent Haar random
unitaries. The signature is to ensure its average is $\mathbb{I}/d$ such
that
Lemma cannot give effective single copy
strategy. According to
Lemma, to distinguish (i) and (ii) with $2/3$
correction rate, which is $\delta= 1/6$ better that $1/2$, we must have
$1/3=2\delta \leq \|\mathbb{E}_{x} p_{\rho_x} - p_{2^{-n}\mathbb I}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$,
where $x$ is an arbitrary distribution on $1,\cdots,M$. It is sufficient
to take the uniform distribution of $x$. Based on
Lemma,
$1/3\leq \|\mathbb{E}_{x} p_{\rho_x} - p_{2^{-n}\mathbb I}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 1 - \min_{l} \mathbb{E}_{x} L_{x}(l)$.
According to the rank-1 reduction in
Lemma, we calculate the leaves'
likelihood $\forall l$ as $$\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}_{x} L_{x}(l) &= \frac{\mathbb{E}_{x} p_{\rho_x}(l)}{p_{2^{-n}\mathbb I}(l)} = \mathbb{E}_{x} \prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{w_{s_t}^{u_t}\bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\rho_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}}{2^{-n}w_{s_t}^{u_t}}=\mathbb{E}_{x} \prod_{t = 1}^T \left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\notag\\
&=\mathbb{E}_{x} \text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T \ln\left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\right]\geq \text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T \mathbb{E}_{x} \ln\left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\right]\notag\\
&=\text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T M^{-1} \ln \left(\prod_{x = 1}^{M/2}\left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\left(1- 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\right)\right]\notag\\
&=\text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T M^{-1} \sum_{x = 1}^{M/2}\ln \left(1- 9\varepsilon^2\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}^2\right)\right] \notag\\
&\geq \text{exp}\left[-9\varepsilon^2\sum_{t = 1}^T \frac{2}{M}\sum_{x = 1}^{M/2} \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}^2\right] \geq \text{exp}\left[-9\varepsilon^2 T \sup_{\ket{\phi}}\frac{2}{M}\sum_{x = 1}^{M/2} \bra{\phi} O_x \ket{\phi}^2\right] \label{eq:sig_canc_TVlb}
\end{align}$$ Here we use $\ln(1 - x)\geq -2x, \forall x \in [0,0.796]$.
This condition is satisfied if and only if
$9\varepsilon^2<0.796, \varepsilon <0.29$. Thus for
$\beta =\text{exp}\left[-9\varepsilon^2 T \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)\right]$,
we have $\text{Pr}_{l \sim p^{(0)}}[L(l) \leq \beta] = 0$, which gives
the inequality use the fact that
$1 - x \leq e^{-x},\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. $$\begin{align}
&1/3\leq 0 +(1 - \beta) = 1 - e^{-9\varepsilon^2 T \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)}  \leq 9\varepsilon^2 T \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M) \notag\\
&\Rightarrow T \geq \Omega(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2 \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)}), \text{~where~} \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M):= \sup_{\ket{\phi}} \frac{2}{M}\sum_{i =1}^{M/2}\bra{\phi} O_i \ket{\phi}^2. \label{eq:LB_shadow_eq}
\end{align}$$ Now we calculate the value $\delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)$. Noted
that the random variable
$\bra{\phi} O_i \ket{\phi},\{O_i\}_i \sim \mathcal{O}$ and
$\bra{\psi_i} Z_n \ket{\psi_i}, \ket{\psi_i} \sim \text{Haar}$ has the
same distribution. Thus, it is sufficient to discuss the property of
function $f(\ket{\psi}):= \bra{\psi} Z_n \ket{\psi}$ with Haar random
inputs.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Lemma

 []{#lemma:expon_cent_ineq label="lemma:expon_cent_ineq"} Given function
$f(\ket{\psi}):= \bra{\psi} Z_n \ket{\psi}$ with independent Haar random
inputs, we conclude that $$\begin{align}
        &\text{Pr}\left[\left|\frac{1}{R}\sum_{i =1}^{R} f(\ket{\psi_i})^2 - \mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi} \sim \text{Haar}}\left[ f(\ket{\psi})^2\right]\right| \geq t\right] \leq 2 e^{-R \min(t^2/\lambda^2, t/\lambda)},\\
        & \text{where~} \lambda = 288\pi^3/2^n,\quad \mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi} \sim \text{Haar}} [f(\ket{\psi_i})^2] = \frac{1}{2^n + 1}
\end{align}$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (Click to expand)

*Proof.* ◻
:::

Now given one state $\ket{\phi}$, we proved that with high probability
$\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2$
will not deviate from its expectation too much, according to the
Lemma. Nevertheless, we hope to prove this
property for all states $\phi$, that is, to bound the deviation of
$\sup_{\ket{\phi}}\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2$.
To do this, to first defined an $\eta$-covering set $\mathcal{N}_{\eta}$
on the n-qubit pure states, as illustrated in
Lemma.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Lemma

 []{#lemma:covering_on_nqubit label="lemma:covering_on_nqubit"} An
$\eta$-covering set $\mathcal{N}_{\eta}$ on the n-qubit pure states is a
finite set of n-qubit pure states such that
$$
\forall \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}_n, \exists \ket{\psi} \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta}, \\
\text{s.t.~} \|\ket{\phi} - \ket{\psi}\|_2 \leq \eta.
$$
The cardinality of $\mathcal{N}_{\eta}$ is upper bounded by
$|\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| \leq (1 + 2/\eta)^{2^{n+1}}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (Click to expand)

*Proof.* The set of n-qubit pure states corresponds to the unit sphere
in the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}(n) \cong \mathbb{C}^{2^n}$. This
complex space of dimension $2^n$ is equivalent to a real space of
dimension $D = 2 \cdot 2^n = 2^{n+1}$. The states are thus points on the
unit sphere $S^{D-1}$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$. Let
$\mathcal{N}_{\eta} = \{\ket{\psi_1}, \ket{\psi_2}, \dots, \ket{\psi_M}\}$
be a maximal set of n-qubit pure states such that the Euclidean distance
between any two distinct states in the set is greater than $\eta$. This
is known as an $\eta$-packing. We first argue that this set
$\mathcal{N}_{\eta}$ is also an $\eta$-covering net. If it were not,
then $\exists \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}_n$ such that
$\forall \ket{\psi_i} \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta} ,\|\ket{\phi} - \ket{\psi_i}\|_2 > \eta$,
which contradicts the assumption that $\mathcal{N}_{\eta}$ is a maximal
set. Therefore, any maximal $\eta$-packing is an $\eta$-covering net.
The problem is now reduced to finding an upper bound on the size
$M = |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}|$ of such a packing. Consider a set of open
balls $\{B(\ket{\psi_i}, \eta/2)\}_{i=1}^M$ of radius $\eta/2$ centered
at each point of our set $\mathcal{N}_{\eta}$. Since for any $i \neq j$,
we have $\|\ket{\psi_i} - \ket{\psi_j}\|_2 > \eta$, the triangle
inequality implies that these balls are disjoint. All these disjoint
balls are contained within a larger ball of radius $1 + \eta/2$ centered
at the origin. This is because each $\ket{\psi_i}$ is on the unit sphere
(norm 1), and any point in the ball $B(\ket{\psi_i}, \eta/2)$ has a norm
of at most $\|\ket{\psi_i}\|_2 + \eta/2 = 1 + \eta/2$. The total volume
of these $M$ disjoint balls cannot exceed the volume of the larger
containing ball. Let $V_D(r)$ be the volume of a $D$-dimensional ball of
radius $r$. We have $\sum_{i=1}^M V_D(\eta/2) \le V_D(1 + \eta/2)$.
Since all the small balls have the same volume, this simplifies to
$M \cdot V_D(\eta/2) \le V_D(1 + \eta/2)$. The volume of a
$D$-dimensional ball of radius $r$ is given by $C_D r^D$ for some
constant $C_D$ that depends only on the dimension $D$. Thus, we can
write $M \cdot C_D (\eta/2)^D \le C_D (1 + \eta/2)^D$. Canceling the
constant $C_D$ and substituting back the dimension $D = 2^{n+1}$, we get
the upper bound on $M$ $$\begin{align}
    |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| = M \le \frac{(1 + \eta/2)^D}{(\eta/2)^D} = \left(\frac{1 + \eta/2}{\eta/2}\right)^D = \left(1 + \frac{2}{\eta}\right)^D.
\end{align}$$ ◻
:::

Then the low-deviation condition that satisfied for arbitrary
$\ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}(n)$ also satisfied on set
$\mathcal{N}_{\eta}$, only with a $|\mathcal{N}_\eta|$ larger error
probability. After this, we show that the function
$g(\ket{\phi}):=\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2$
is Lipschitz continuous, which means that the difference of function
value is upper bounded by the variables difference. Combining the
Lipschitz continuity and the property of the $\eta$-covering, we show
upper bounds for the value
$\sup_{\ket{\phi}}\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2$,
as rigrously illustrated in
Lemma.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Lemma

 []{#lemma:point_to_uniform label="lemma:point_to_uniform"} Given an
L-Lipschitz continuous function $f:V \to \mathbb{R}$ on metric space $V$
and an $\eta$-covering set $\mathcal{N}_{\eta}$ of $V$, if
$\forall x \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta}, |f(x) - c| < t$, then
$\forall x \in V, |f(x) - c| < t + L \eta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (Click to expand)

*Proof.* By definition, we know that
$\forall x \in V, \exists r_x \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta} \text{~s.t.~} |r_x - x| \leq \eta$.
Then we conclude $$\begin{align}
        \forall x \in V, |f(x) - c| &\leq |f(x) - f(r_x)| + |f(r_x) - c|\leq L\|x - r_x\| + t \leq L\eta + t.
\end{align}$$ ◻
:::

If we further

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Theorem

Given a uniform distribution on $M$ Pauli observables
$\mathcal{A}:=\{P_1,\cdots,P_M\}$, any single-copy learning algorithm
that predict $\{\text{tr}(\rho P)\}_{P \sim \mathcal{A}}$ with
$\varepsilon$-additive error and $2/3$ success probability must use
$T \geq \Omega \left(\varepsilon^{-2} \min\{M/\log M, 2^n\}\right)$
samples.
:::

## Pauli mixed states

::: problem
[]{#prob:Pauli_mixed_test label="prob:Pauli_mixed_test"} Given a subset
$\mathcal{O} \subset \mathcal{P}(n)$, try to discriminate (i). A set of
state
${S}_{\mathcal{O}}:=\{\sigma_{P}:=(\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon P)/d\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}}$
and (ii) $\rho = \mathbb{I}/2^n$ with confidence $1 - \delta$.
:::

## Single replica.

Similarly, we set up hard distributions as uniform distribution on
signed Pauli operators $\{+1,-1\}\times \mathcal{O}$, where
$\mathcal{O} \subset \{\mathbb{I},X,Y,Z\}$. Follow the same procedure of
Eq.~(eq:sig_canc_TVlb), we then calculate its rank-1 POVM leaves
likelihood as: $$\begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}_{s,P} L_{s,P}(l)  \geq \exp\left[-18\varepsilon^2T \sup_{\ket{\phi}} \mathbb{E}_{P\in \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{O})} \bra{\phi} P \ket{\phi}^2\right].
\end{align}$$ In the case of $\mathcal{O} = \mathcal{P}_n$, we use the
identity
$$
\mathbb{E}_{P\in \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{P}_n)} \bra{\phi} P \ket{\phi}^2 \\
=\bra{\phi}\bra{\phi} 4^{-n}\sum_{P\in \mathcal{P}_n}P \otimes P\ket{\phi}\ket{\phi}
$$
and
$\sum_{P\in \mathcal{P}_n}P \otimes P = 2^{n}\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}$.
We conclude that
$\mathbb{E}_{s,P} L_{s,P}(l) \geq e^{-18\varepsilon^2 T 2^{-n}},\forall l$.
Use Lemma, we conclude that for all choice of
single-copy POVM,
$\|p_{\mathbb{I}/d} - \mathbb{E}_{s,P}p_{\rho_{s,P}}\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \leq 1 - e^{-18\varepsilon^2 T 2^{-n}}$.
This means that to reach confidence $1/2 + \delta/2$, we have to set
$1 - e^{-18\varepsilon^2 T 2^{-n}} \geq \delta \Rightarrow T \geq 18^{-1}\times 2^n \varepsilon^{-2}\ln(1 - \delta)$.

According to
Theorem, we can also calculate its
$\chi$-squared divergence given ensemble $\mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}$ on
the subset of Pauli operators $\mathcal{O}$: $$\begin{align}
    \delta_{\mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} &:= \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma_P F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2= \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s}  \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{d}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon P}{d}F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})/d} - 1\right]^2 \notag\\
    &= 9\varepsilon^2 \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s}  \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{d}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}({P}F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}\right]^2 = {9\varepsilon^2} \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s} \frac{\left[\mathrm{tr}({P}F_{s})\right]^2}{{d}\cdot \mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}.
\end{align}$$ Since $F_s$ includes all the rank-1 POVMs and each POVMs
with rank greater than 1 can be equivalently realized using rank-1 POVMs
with undecreasing discrimination efficiency, as shown in
Lemma. We can plug in
$F_s = 2^{n}w_s \ket{\psi_s}\!\bra{\psi_s}$ with $\{w_s\}$ a valid
distribution and conclude the same result: $$\begin{align}
    \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s} \frac{\left[\mathrm{tr}({P}F_{s})\right]^2}{{d}\cdot \mathrm{tr}(F_{s})} &= \max_{\ket{\psi_s}}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s}w_s{\left[\bra{\psi_s}{P}\ket{\psi_s}\right]^2} = \max_{\ket{\phi}}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} {\bra{\phi}{P}\ket{\phi}^2}
    \\
    &\sim \Omega(2^{-n}) \text{~if~} \mathcal{O} = \mathcal{P}_n, \mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{O}} = \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{O}).
\end{align}$$ Then based on
Lemma, $T\geq 2^n$. Note that such a
martingale analysis do not directly applied to purity-identity test,
which has a constant $\chi$-squared divergence, as calculated below:
$$\begin{align}
    \delta_{\mathrm{Haar}} &= \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s}  \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{d}\mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi}\sim \mathrm{Haar}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})/d} - 1\right]^2=\max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s}  \mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}^{\otimes 2}F_{s}\otimes F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})/d}\right]- 1\\
    &=\max_{\ket{\psi_s} }\sum_{s}   d^2w_s\mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi}} \left[{\mathrm{tr}({\psi}^{\otimes 2} \psi_s^{\otimes 2})}\right]- 1 = \frac{2d^2}{d(d+1)} - 1 = \frac{d-1}{d+1} \sim \Omega(1).
\end{align}$$ This great difference between ensemble supports on
$\{(\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon O)/2^n\}_{O \in \mathcal{O}}$ and Haar
random state supports on $\{\psi\}$ is because the probability of the
latter one is more concentrated. $$\begin{align*}
    p_{\mathrm{Haar}}(\psi_s) =\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}\psi_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{I}/d\cdot \psi_{s})}= d |\langle {\psi}|{\psi_s}\rangle|^2 \in[0,d], \, p_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_s) =\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon P}{d}\psi_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{I}/d\psi_{s})}=1 + 3\varepsilon\langle{\psi_s}|P|{\psi_s}\rangle \in [1- 3\varepsilon, 1+ 3\varepsilon].
\end{align*}$$

## Single Replica with Clifford Restriction {#sec-single-clifford}

When restricted to single-copy ($c=1$) measurements within the Clifford group, the discrimination power is severely limited. This setting corresponds to classical shadows with Clifford measurements.

For the Pauli-mixed ensemble $\{(\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon P)/d\}_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n}$, single-copy Clifford measurements achieve:
$$\begin{align}
    \max_{\ket{\psi} \in \mathrm{Stab}_n} \mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{P}_n} \bra{\psi}P\ket{\psi}^2 = \frac{1}{2^n}
\end{align}$$
since stabilizer states have flat Pauli spectrum (each non-identity Pauli has expectation $\pm 1$ or $0$, and the average over the Pauli group vanishes for stabilizer states).

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Consequence

Single-copy Clifford measurements require $T = \Omega(2^n/\varepsilon^2)$ samples to distinguish $(\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon P)/d$ from $\mathbb{I}/d$, matching the information-theoretic lower bound up to constants.
:::

## Multi-Replica with Bounded Memory {#sec-multi-replica-memory}

When multiple copies are available but quantum memory is bounded, there is a tradeoff between the number of copies processed jointly and the total sample complexity.

Consider strategies that process at most $c$ copies jointly with $k$ qubits of quantum memory between rounds. The key constraint is:
$$\begin{align}
    \mathcal{M}^{k}_{c,n} := \left\{\{F_s\}_s : F_s \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes c}), \, \mathrm{rank}(\sum_s F_s \otimes \ket{s}\bra{s}) \leq 2^k \right\}
\end{align}$$

This captures the scenario where the post-measurement classical description is bounded, limiting the information that can be carried forward to subsequent rounds.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Lemma (Memory-Sample Tradeoff)

For distinguishing states from the Pauli-mixed ensemble with bounded memory $k$ and $c$-copy measurements:
$$\begin{align}
    T \geq \frac{2^n}{2^{k + c \cdot n/(c+1)}}
\end{align}$$
:::

This interpolates between the single-copy bound ($c=1$: $T \geq 2^{n/2 - k}$) and the multi-copy regime where entangled measurements can achieve polynomial scaling.
